newsitem.title: DENMARK: SAS says profitability in "critical" state.
newsitem.headline: SAS says profitability in "critical" state.

text.p: Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) had static earnings but a three percent rise in spending during the first half of 1996 and would have to increase productivity and freeze employment to restore itself to health, a company executive said.

"Imagine that was your private financial situation, it's bad business. The situation is critically negative," Scandinavian routes manager Knut Solberg wrote in the current issue of company magazine SAS Inside, received by Reuters on Monday.
SAS has already said that it does not expect to match 1995's record pre-tax profit of 2.6 billion Swedish crowns in 1996.
But Solberg said that falling profitability was a warning light for the carrier, a former monopoly jointly owned by the Danish, Norwegian and Swedish governments and private investors.

"We have seen weaker traffic growth, falling earnings per kilometre flown, modest productivity gains and a sharp rise in expenditure...the payroll grew by about 2,000 people between January and August this year."

"In future we must achieve productivity growth without adding a single new employee," he said, adding that the airline had to fight hard to meet the challenge of competition arising from deregulation of the industry.

Danish franchise British Airways Express and Brussels-based Virgin Express are challenging SAS in Europe, between Nordic countries and on Danish domestic routes and Norway's Braathens SAFE offers an alternative for travellers between Oslo and the Swedish capital, Stockholm.

"That is one of SAS' best routes and Braathens is now coming in with seven round trips daily. If Braathens only takes 20-25 percent of traffic from us, then our profits on that route are nil! That shows how tough it is," Solberg said.
Another competitor is A.P. Moeller unit Maersk Air.

The former domestic airline, one of the first in Europe to go international after 1984 EU deregulation, ran full-page colour newspaper advertisements on Monday promoting improved business class comfort on its Copenhagen-London flights.
SAS has been the butt of criticism for its timekeeping, service and cramped business class seating on short-haul flights. --Steve Weizman, Copenhagen newsroom +45 33969650
